title: In 101 amniote genomes, the 1.5-fold LINE-1 excess on the eutherian X matches the LINE excess on bird Z chromosomes, which have no X inactivation
abstract: The X chromosome of placental mammals has about 1.5 times more LINE-1 retrotransposon DNA than its autosomes, and the Z chromosome of neognath birds, which have no X inactivation, has an excess of the same size of its own LINE family (CR1). So this excess forms without X inactivation, and it alone cannot support the Lyon repeat hypothesis, which gives this large class of non-coding DNA a function: to help spread the silencing of one X in female mammals. LINEs are transposable elements that copy themselves through RNA; LINE-1 makes about 17-20% of mammal genomes. We used uniform repeat annotations (UCSC GenArk RepeatMasker) of 101 chromosome-level genomes. In 1-Mb windows, we compared repeat coverage on the X or Z with the coverage that a model fitted on the autosomes of the same genome predicts from GC content, chromosome length, distance to the chromosome end and CpG-island density. The median excess of the most abundant LINE was 1.54-fold on the eutherian X (LINE-1; 30 species, 19 orders) and 1.48-fold on the neognath Z (CR1; 41 species, 35 orders); the difference was -0.008 log2 units (95% CI -0.12 to +0.11), and equivalence tests excluded differences larger than about 0.10-0.15 log2 units. In both groups the excess was in younger subfamilies and in longer elements (exploratory). On the X, the class-level excess was specific to LINE-1, but long LTR elements also had an excess; at matched length the gap between LINE-1 and LTR elements narrowed but did not close. The group median excesses were larger than the maximum (4/3) that sex-biased insertion alone can make. Not all sex chromosomes had a large excess: the marsupial X (imprinted X inactivation) had a modest LINE-1 excess (1.15-fold raw, 1.3-1.5-fold after GC adjustment), and monotreme X and squamate sex chromosomes had little excess of their most abundant LINE. Relative to the scatter among its own autosomes, the eutherian X was more extreme than the bird Z (median z 5.9 vs 3.0). Each group descends from one sex-chromosome origin, so the comparison is a pattern, not a replicated experiment. The analysis does not test mechanistic roles of LINE-1 RNA in X inactivation. Repeat libraries differ between species, pseudoautosomal regions were not removed, and 20 of 121 selected assemblies could not be analysed.

display.caption: Excess of the most abundant LINE on the X or Z chromosome (log2 observed / expected from autosomes of the same GC, length and CpG density), one dot per species. Eutherian X (LINE-1) and neognath bird Z (CR1) have the same median excess; birds have no X inactivation. Filled dots: the sex chromosome scores higher than every comparable autosome.

Exploratory: raw sex-chromosome-to-autosome density by element length. On the eutherian X, both LINE-1 and LTR elements show an excess that rises with length; short solo LTRs, which make most LTR DNA, have none; LINE-1 stays above LTR at most matched lengths. On the bird Z, CR1 rises with length up to 2-4 kb.

Sex-chromosome-to-autosome density of the most abundant LINE by subfamily age quintile, for genomes whose repeat library resolves young subfamilies. In eutherians and in neognath birds, the excess is in younger subfamilies and absent in the oldest fifth.
